title: What is Epsilon GC (no-op collector), and when is it useful (benchmarking, short-lived programs, allocation-rate analysis)?
shortTitle: What Epsilon GC is — the no-op collector — and when it is useful

s1_definition.profdef: Epsilon is a no-op, or passive, garbage collector introduced in Java 11 via JEP 318. It handles memory allocation but never reclaims any memory — it does no marking, no relocation, and no collection. When the heap is exhausted, the JVM simply stops: depending on configuration it throws OutOfMemoryError or terminates. It is an experimental collector enabled with `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC`, meant for performance testing, very short-lived jobs, and measuring allocation behaviour, not for general production.
s1_definition.analogy: Epsilon is like a bank that gives out desks to every new customer but never clears any desk. As long as the floor has free desks everything is fast and there is zero cleaning-crew interruption. The moment the floor is full, the bank just closes the doors — it does not shuffle anyone around. You would only run the bank this way to measure exactly how fast desks fill up, or for a pop-up event that you know will end before the floor is full.
s1_definition.oneliner: Epsilon allocates but never collects — the heap only grows until it is full and the JVM stops — and that makes it perfect for benchmarking allocation and running tiny short-lived jobs with zero GC overhead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Epsilon is a no-op, or passive, garbage collector introduced in Java 11 via JEP 318. It handles memory allocation but never reclaims any memory — it does no marking, no relocation, and no collection. When the heap is exhausted, the JVM simply stops: depending on configuration it throws OutOfMemoryError or terminates. It is an experimental collector enabled with `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC`, meant for performance testing, very short-lived jobs, and measuring allocation behaviour, not for general production.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Epsilon is like a bank that gives out desks to every new customer but never clears any desk. As long as the floor has free desks everything is fast and there is zero cleaning-crew interruption. The moment the floor is full, the bank just closes the doors — it does not shuffle anyone around. You would only run the bank this way to measure exactly how fast desks fill up, or for a pop-up event that you know will end before the floor is full.

**One line to remember:** Epsilon allocates but never collects — the heap only grows until it is full and the JVM stops — and that makes it perfect for benchmarking allocation and running tiny short-lived jobs with zero GC overhead.

sections.s2_technical:
Epsilon implements the full garbage-collector interface the JVM expects, but its collection logic is empty. It allocates objects by bumping a pointer through the heap, which is about as fast as allocation can get, and it tracks nothing for reclamation. There are no GC threads, no barriers, no pauses, and essentially no CPU or memory overhead beyond allocation itself. When the heap runs out, Epsilon cannot free anything, so the JVM throws an OutOfMemoryError, and you can configure it to dump the heap or exit on that event.

The most common legitimate use is performance benchmarking. If you want to measure the raw cost of your code without any garbage-collection noise, Epsilon removes GC from the picture entirely, so your microbenchmark numbers reflect only allocation and your logic. It also lets you measure your application's true allocation rate: run a fixed workload under Epsilon with a known heap size and see how quickly the heap fills, which tells you how much garbage the code produces per unit of work — valuable input for choosing and tuning a real collector.

A second use is very short-lived programs. A small command-line tool, a one-shot batch job, or a serverless function that starts, does a bounded amount of work, and exits may never allocate enough to exhaust a generously sized heap. For such jobs, paying for a real collector's threads and barriers is pure overhead; Epsilon gives maximum throughput and the lowest possible latency because it literally never pauses, and the process exits before the heap would fill.

A third use is as a last-resort pressure test: running under Epsilon makes memory leaks and excessive allocation obvious and fast, because anything that would normally be collected now accumulates until the JVM dies, so a leak that a real collector would hide shows up immediately.

Epsilon is explicitly not for general production services, which run indefinitely and must reclaim memory. It is experimental and gated behind the unlock flag. The senior nuance is that Epsilon is a measurement and specialization tool: you reach for it to isolate GC from an experiment, to size heaps from measured allocation rates, or to squeeze a known-bounded job, and you pair it with `-Xlog:gc` and heap dumps so that when it does hit OutOfMemoryError you capture the allocation story.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's performance team needs to measure the exact allocation cost of the interest-calculation routine without garbage-collection noise polluting the numbers. This is exactly what Epsilon is for — with no collector running, the measured time and the heap-fill rate reflect only the code.

Problem 2 — The same routine is suspected of allocating far more than necessary per account. By running it under Epsilon with a known heap and counting how many accounts it processes before OutOfMemoryError, the team can compute bytes-per-account precisely. This is allocation-rate analysis.

Our mini-project is a runnable allocation-rate probe: it processes a stream of interest calculations, periodically reports heap used so you can see the monotonic growth with no collection, and is designed to be run under Epsilon. Classes are `InterestAllocationProbe` (driver), `InterestCalculation` (the per-account allocator under test), and `GrowthReporter` (logs heap used to show the straight-line growth Epsilon produces).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
epsilon-probe/
├── pom.xml
├── run.sh
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/epsilon/
            ├── InterestAllocationProbe.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── GrowthReporter.java
```

Configuration (JVM flags):

```bash
# epsilon-flags.conf — passive collector for measurement only
-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions
-XX:+UseEpsilonGC
-Xms512m -Xmx512m                 # fixed small heap so it fills in a measurable time
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError    # capture what accumulated when it dies
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,tags
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Run under Epsilon — observe straight-line heap growth then a clean OOM
java -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC \
     -Xms512m -Xmx512m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/epsilon-probe-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.epsilon.InterestAllocationProbe

# Compare: the SAME program under G1 never OOMs because retained is the only live set
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms512m -Xmx512m \
     -cp target/epsilon-probe-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.epsilon.InterestAllocationProbe   # will run much longer
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a loop that computes monthly interest for an unbounded sequence of accounts, run under Epsilon with a fixed five-hundred-twelve-megabyte heap.

Step 1. Each iteration calls `calculateFor`, which allocates several intermediate BigDecimal objects and a String label. Under a real collector the ones not retained would be collected; under Epsilon nothing is ever collected.

Step 2. The result BigDecimal is added to the `retained` list, which grows forever. But even the intermediate objects that are not retained stay in the heap because Epsilon does not reclaim.

Step 3. Every hundred thousand accounts, `GrowthReporter` logs heap used. Under Epsilon this number only ever goes up — a clean monotonic line — because there is no collection to pull it back down. That straight line is the visual signature of a no-op collector.

Step 4. The heap approaches five hundred twelve megabytes. Epsilon cannot free anything, so the next allocation that does not fit triggers an OutOfMemoryError, and because the flag is set, a heap dump is written.

Step 5. The catch block logs how many accounts were processed before the heap filled. `summarize` divides the heap size by the account count to estimate bytes allocated per account — the allocation-rate measurement the team wanted.

Step 6. Running the same program under G1 for comparison shows it does not OOM anywhere near as fast, because G1 reclaims the unretained intermediates; the only genuinely live set is the retained list. The contrast makes the role of a collector obvious.

```
Oct 25, 2026 1:48:05 AM com.bank.jvm.epsilon.InterestAllocationProbe main

Oct 25, 2026 1:48:05 AM com.bank.jvm.epsilon.InterestAllocationProbe main

Oct 25, 2026 1:48:05 AM com.bank.jvm.epsilon.GrowthReporter report
INFO: Processed 100000 accounts, heap used=112MB (monotonic — no GC under Epsilon)
Oct 25, 2026 1:48:06 AM com.bank.jvm.epsilon.GrowthReporter report
INFO: Processed 300000 accounts, heap used=341MB (monotonic — no GC under Epsilon)
Oct 25, 2026 1:48:06 AM com.bank.jvm.epsilon.InterestAllocationProbe main
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Loop: calculateFor(account) ×N
    │
    ▼
  Allocate BigDecimals + String label  (bump pointer, zero GC overhead)
    │
    ▼
  retained.add(interest)   ← keeps growing forever
    │
    ▼
  Heap used ──────────────────────────────→ straight-line growth (NO collection)
    │                                           │
    │  Epsilon: no mark, no sweep, no relocate  │
    ▼                                           ▼
  Heap reaches -Xmx (512MB)              GrowthReporter logs monotonic rise
    │
    ▼
  next allocation doesn't fit → OutOfMemoryError → heap dump
    │
    ▼
  summarize(): bytes/account = heap / accounts   ← the measurement goal
```

```
  4.   every 100k → reporter.report  → monotonic used MB
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Epsilon is the no-op or passive garbage collector, introduced in Java 11 as an experimental feature behind the unlock flag. It implements the collector interface the JVM requires, but its collection logic is empty: it allocates by simply bumping a pointer through the heap, which is the fastest allocation possible, and it never marks, never relocates, and never reclaims anything. There are no GC threads, no barriers, and essentially no pauses, so it has the lowest possible runtime overhead. The catch is that when the heap fills, Epsilon cannot free anything, so the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError, and you normally pair it with heap-dump-on-out-of-memory to capture what accumulated.

Because it removes garbage collection entirely, Epsilon is excellent for three things. First, benchmarking: when you want a microbenchmark to reflect only your code and allocation cost with zero GC noise, Epsilon gives you that clean signal. Second, allocation-rate analysis: run a known workload under Epsilon with a fixed heap, see how fast the heap fills or how many units of work complete before OutOfMemoryError, and you get a precise bytes-per-operation figure that helps you size and choose a real collector. Third, very short-lived programs — a small tool, a one-shot batch, or a serverless function that finishes before it would ever fill a generous heap — where paying for a real collector's machinery is pure overhead and Epsilon delivers maximum throughput with no pauses.

What Epsilon is not is a production collector for long-running services, which must reclaim memory to run indefinitely. At National Bank of India I used Epsilon to measure the interest-calculation routine: running it under a fixed heap with everything retained let me read the heap-fill rate as a clean straight line and compute exactly how many bytes the routine allocated per account, which told us it was allocating far more intermediate objects than necessary. We optimized the routine on the strength of that measurement and then ran the service in production under G1. So I treat Epsilon as a precise laboratory instrument for isolating and measuring allocation, not as something you would ever leave running under real traffic.
